messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0024-reverse-118", "row_sha256": "e84401ea2bc528c3f67aa9edcdb135126cc81fb5357421a41a4826b87517a897", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "we need a prompt put in order for the small exhibit brief, not the exhibit text itself yet. this is for Alderwick Local Museum and the working title is “Across in Five Minutes.” the exhibit is about the North Quay foot ferry, which crossed the Alderwick canal between Market Steps on the east bank and Foundry Quay on the west bank. The service began in 1958 and ended in 1994. A road bridge opened that same year; our notes establish the dates but do not say the bridge alone caused the ferry to close, so don’t present that as settled. The planned display is in the museum’s small ground-floor room from October 2026 through May 2027. The intended visitors include Alderwick residents who remember the ferry, families, and people who have never heard of it. Please write a clear, welcoming gallery brief that gives those visitors a way into the story without assuming they already know the waterfront.

The actual request is for a draft of about 450 words of introductory gallery text, plus three short object captions, each about 45–60 words. Keep the introduction and captions together as one draft, but make it clear which is which. The introduction should explain what crossed the canal, where the two landings were, and the service dates. It should bring out how the crossing fitted into everyday routines, while distinguishing the interview memories from facts confirmed in the museum records. Avoid turning it into a general history of Alderwick or an argument that the ferry was better than the bridge. There is no need for a separate press release, school activity, or design plan. Please send the first draft to Leonie, not Ellis.

Some source notes to work from: the museum’s bound operating ledger has entries for the ferry from 1958 to 1994, though the surviving volume has gaps in 1967 and 1968. The ledger records two-person crews on ordinary weekdays in 1972, and a fare of 8 pence for an adult crossing in that year. It does not identify every passenger or give a full daily timetable. A 1981 council map labels the east-bank landing “Market Steps” and the west-bank landing “Foundry Quay.” The map shows the footpath from Market Steps reaching the old market street, and the path from Foundry Quay meeting Foundry Lane. A small brass bell from the ferry is in the collection, accession number ALM.2003.17; it was donated by Mara Vale in 2003. The collection record says the bell hung beside the operator’s seat, but does not give the date it was installed. There is also a paper adult ticket dated 14 June 1982, with “8p” printed on it. The ticket was found inside a ledger donated by former clerk Peter Doran; the record does not say who used it.

We have two recorded interviews, both conducted by museum volunteer Nisha Patel. One is with Mara Vale, recorded 3 June 2025; the other is with Tom Arlen, recorded 19 July 2025. Use these supplied excerpts as interview memories, not as proof of details the records do not establish. Mara said, “Dad took the ferry to the early shift when the tide path was flooded. If the bell went twice, you knew there was room for one more person.” Tom said, “We called it the five-minute boat, though nobody timed it. I carried my school shoes in a bag because the landing could be muddy.” Don’t suggest that both interviewees describe the same trip or that the quoted details apply to every passenger. Keep the words inside each quote exactly as supplied if you include them. The interviews do not give a precise crossing time, explain the bell signal formally, or say what happened to the boat after 1994.

For the three captions, use the brass bell, the 1982 ticket, and the 1981 council map, one object per caption. Keep caption claims close to the collection and map notes above. The map can help visitors locate both landings, but don’t imply it shows a ferry route or the position of the boat. Mention the accession number in the bell caption. The ticket caption can state its printed fare and date, but should not assign it to an identified passenger. You can point out that the exhibit combines objects, records, and oral memories, as long as the distinction stays clear. Please don’t invent a name for the ferry, a boat design, an exact crossing duration, passenger totals, or a reason for closure that our notes don’t provide.

Tone should be plain, specific, and warm without sounding sentimental. Short sentences are fine, but don’t make the visitors feel that they have to know local family names or ferry terminology. The title is a working title, not a confirmed historical name for the service. Keep the draft usable as gallery text rather than addressing the visitor as if this were a tour script. The closing of the service in 1994 and the opening of the road bridge in that year may both be mentioned, but make their relationship no stronger than the records support. The final piece should leave room for visitors’ own memories without claiming that everyone in town used the ferry. We need the brief to give a careful account of the available material, including where it has gaps, and still feel readable in a small room.", "output": "Prepare a draft gallery brief for Alderwick Local Museum’s small ground-floor room, where the planned exhibit will be on display from October 2026 through May 2027. The working title is “Across in Five Minutes.” The exhibit concerns the North Quay foot ferry, which crossed the Alderwick canal between Market Steps on the east bank and Foundry Quay on the west bank. The service began in 1958 and ended in 1994. A road bridge opened in 1994 as well, but the available notes do not establish that the bridge alone caused the ferry to close.

Write approximately 450 words of introductory gallery text and three object captions of about 45–60 words each. Present the introduction and captions together as one draft, clearly identifying each part. The intended visitors include Alderwick residents who remember the ferry, families, and people who have never heard of it. Explain what crossed the canal, where the two landings were, and the service dates. Show how the crossing fitted into everyday routines while distinguishing interview memories from facts confirmed in museum records. Keep the text welcoming and accessible to visitors unfamiliar with the waterfront. Use a plain, specific, warm tone without sentimentality; the text should work as gallery text, not as a tour script. Do not turn it into a general history of Alderwick or argue that the ferry was better than the bridge. There is no need for a press release, school activity, or design plan.

Use the following source notes:

- The museum’s bound operating ledger has ferry entries from 1958 to 1994, with gaps in the surviving volume for 1967 and 1968. It records two-person crews on ordinary weekdays in 1972 and an adult fare of 8 pence that year. It does not identify every passenger or provide a complete daily timetable.
- A 1981 council map labels the east-bank landing “Market Steps” and the west-bank landing “Foundry Quay.” It shows the path from Market Steps reaching the old market street and the path from Foundry Quay meeting Foundry Lane. It does not show a ferry route or the boat’s position.
- A brass ferry bell, accession number ALM.2003.17, was donated by Mara Vale in 2003. Its collection record says it hung beside the operator’s seat but does not date when it was installed.
- A paper adult ticket dated 14 June 1982 is printed “8p.” It was found inside a ledger donated by former clerk Peter Doran; the record does not identify its user.

The museum has two recorded interviews, both conducted by volunteer Nisha Patel: Mara Vale’s interview was recorded 3 June 2025, and Tom Arlen’s was recorded 19 July 2025. Treat the following excerpts as interview memories, not as proof of details absent from the records. If included, reproduce the words inside the quotations exactly:

- Mara: “Dad took the ferry to the early shift when the tide path was flooded. If the bell went twice, you knew there was room for one more person.”
- Tom: “We called it the five-minute boat, though nobody timed it. I carried my school shoes in a bag because the landing could be muddy.”

Do not imply that the interviewees describe the same trip or that their memories apply to every passenger. The interviews do not establish an exact crossing time, a formal explanation of the bell signal, or what happened to the boat after 1994.

Include three captions, one each for the brass bell, the 1982 ticket, and the 1981 council map. Keep their claims close to the collection and map notes. Mention accession number ALM.2003.17 in the bell caption. The ticket caption may state its printed fare and date but must not assign it to an identified passenger. You may note that the exhibit combines objects, records, and oral memories, while keeping those source types distinct.

Do not invent a ferry name, boat design, exact crossing duration, passenger totals, or a closure reason unsupported by the notes. The title is a working title, not a confirmed historical name for the service. The closing of the ferry and opening of the road bridge may both be mentioned, but do not claim a stronger relationship than the records support. Leave room for visitors’ own memories without suggesting that everyone in town used the ferry. Give a careful, readable account of the available material, including its gaps. Send the first draft to Leonie, not Ellis."}]
